cards.q: What does physiology study?
cards.a: How living organisms and their parts function.
options: The chemical composition of body fluids only
The shape and location of body structures
How living organisms and their parts function
The classification of organisms into groups
cards.explanation: Physiology is the study of function: how molecules, cells, organs, and whole organisms work and how that work is regulated. Chemical composition is one tool physiology uses, not its definition. Shape and location define anatomy, which is a partner discipline rather than the same field. Classification of organisms is taxonomy and answers a different question entirely.

cards.q: Which level of organization sits immediately above the tissue level?
cards.a: Organ.
options: Cell
Organ
Organ system
Organelle
cards.explanation: Two or more tissue types combine into an organ, so organ is the next step up from tissue. Cell and organelle both sit below tissue, since cells are the units that make tissues. Organ system is one level higher still, made of several organs that share a common function.

cards.q: What defines a tissue?
cards.a: A group of similar cells and their surrounding material that carry out a shared function.
options: Any structure made of more than one cell type
A group of similar cells and their surrounding material that carry out a shared function
A membrane bound compartment inside a cell
A set of organs that cooperate on one task
cards.explanation: A tissue is defined by similar cells working together on one function, together with the extracellular material they secrete. Simply having more than one cell type describes an organ, not a tissue. A membrane bound compartment inside a cell is an organelle, one level down. A set of cooperating organs is an organ system, two levels up.

cards.q: What is the smallest unit of the body that can carry out all the basic processes of life on its own?
cards.a: The cell.
options: The organelle
The cell
The protein
The tissue
cards.explanation: The cell is the smallest structure that can take in nutrients, produce energy, respond to signals, and reproduce, so it is the basic unit of life. An organelle performs one job but cannot survive independently. A protein is a molecule and depends entirely on the cell around it. A tissue is larger than the minimum, since it is many cells together.

cards.q: Which of these is an organ system?
cards.a: The cardiovascular system.
options: The cardiovascular system
The heart
Cardiac muscle
A cardiac myocyte
cards.explanation: An organ system is a set of organs that cooperate on one large function, and the heart plus the blood vessels plus the blood make up the cardiovascular system. Cardiac muscle is a tissue. The heart alone is a single organ. A cardiac myocyte is one cell, the lowest of these four levels.

cards.q: An emergent property is best described as a property that appears at which point?
cards.a: When simpler parts are combined, and that none of the parts shows alone.
options: Only in diseased tissue and never in healthy tissue
When simpler parts are combined, and that none of the parts shows alone
Whenever a molecule changes its chemical shape
Only when an organ is removed from the body and studied alone
cards.explanation: Emergent properties arise from the interaction of parts, so consciousness or a heartbeat exists at the assembled level but not in any single molecule or cell. Disease is not required, since most emergent properties are normal. A shape change in one molecule is a molecular event, not an emergent one. Isolating an organ removes interactions and tends to hide emergent properties rather than reveal them.

cards.q: What does pathophysiology study?
cards.a: How normal function is altered by disease.
options: The structure of diseased organs at autopsy
How normal function is altered by disease
The naming and classification of diseases
The drugs used to treat a given disease
cards.explanation: Pathophysiology asks how the normal mechanisms of function break down or shift during disease, which is why it builds directly on physiology. Studying the structure of diseased organs is pathological anatomy. Naming and classifying diseases is nosology. Drug treatment belongs to pharmacology and therapeutics.

cards.q: Hemoglobin binding an oxygen molecule is an event at which level of organization?
cards.a: Molecular.
options: Molecular
Cellular
Organ
Tissue
cards.explanation: One protein binding one gas molecule is a chemical interaction between molecules, so the event itself is molecular. Cellular would be the red blood cell carrying that hemoglobin. Tissue and organ levels involve many cells working together, which is where the consequence of oxygen binding shows up but not where the binding occurs.

cards.q: A researcher measures how fast a single isolated intestinal epithelial cell takes up glucose. At what level of organization is this measurement made?
cards.a: Cellular.
options: Molecular
Tissue
Cellular
Organ
cards.explanation: The unit being measured is one whole cell performing a function, which places the measurement at the cellular level. Molecular would be the behavior of the SGLT transporter protein by itself. Tissue would be a sheet of epithelium, and organ would be the intestine as a whole, both of which involve many cells acting together.

cards.q: Swallowing moves food from the mouth through the pharynx and esophagus into the stomach. Which level of organization best explains this process?
cards.a: Organ system.
options: Cellular
Molecular
Organ system
Tissue
cards.explanation: Swallowing requires several organs acting in a coordinated sequence, which is exactly what an organ system does, so the digestive system level is the right one. Cellular and molecular events certainly occur in each muscle fiber, but neither one explains the ordered movement from one organ to the next. A single tissue cannot produce a sequence spanning three separate organs.

cards.q: A student says that the left ventricle generates enough pressure to eject blood into the aorta. This statement describes function at which level?
cards.a: Organ.
options: Tissue
Organ system
Cellular
Organ
cards.explanation: The left ventricle is one chamber of the heart and the heart is a single organ, so pressure generation by the ventricle is organ level function. Tissue level would describe cardiac muscle contracting. Cellular level would describe a myocyte shortening. Organ system level would include the vessels and the blood, not the ventricle alone.

cards.q: Insulin binds its receptor on a liver cell and changes the shape of the receptor protein. Where does this event belong?
cards.a: The molecular level.
options: The tissue level
The molecular level
The organ level
The organ system level
cards.explanation: A hormone and a receptor are both molecules, and the binding event is a change in molecular shape, so it is molecular. Tissue and organ levels describe what the liver does after the signal is received, such as storing glucose. The organ system level would describe the endocrine control of blood glucose across the whole body.

cards.q: Sheets of alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium next to them form the surface across which gases diffuse in the lung. That diffusion surface is best described at which level?
cards.a: Tissue.
options: Organelle
Molecular
Organ system
Tissue
cards.explanation: Two thin layers of similar cells acting as one barrier is a tissue level description of the respiratory membrane. Organelle and molecular levels are far too small to describe a diffusion surface. Organ system would be the whole respiratory system including airways and the muscles of breathing.

cards.q: Body temperature stays near 37 C while a person runs on a hot day, because skin blood flow, sweating, and behavior all change together. Which level best explains that stability?
cards.a: The organism level.
options: The cellular level
The organism level
The tissue level
The molecular level
cards.explanation: Stability produced by several systems adjusting at once is a whole body outcome, so it is best explained at the organism level. Cellular and molecular events such as sweat gland secretion or channel opening are the machinery, not the explanation for the coordinated result. A single tissue cannot integrate blood flow, sweating, and behavior.

cards.q: Which question is a physiology question rather than an anatomy question?
cards.a: Why does the ventricle wall thicken when arterial pressure stays high?
options: How many chambers does the human heart have?
Why does the ventricle wall thicken when arterial pressure stays high?
Where do the coronary arteries branch from the aorta?
Which vessel leaves the left ventricle?
cards.explanation: Asking why a structure changes in response to a load is asking about function and regulation, which is physiology. Counting chambers, naming the vessel that leaves the ventricle, and locating a branch point are all descriptions of structure and position, which is anatomy. Anatomy supplies the map that physiology then explains.

cards.q: Sinoatrial node cells removed from the heart and kept in a dish fire about 100 times per minute, but the same person at rest has a heart rate near 70 beats per minute. Which level of organization explains the difference?
cards.a: The organ system level, because autonomic input to the intact heart slows the node.
options: The organ system level, because autonomic input to the intact heart slows the node
The molecular level, because the ion channels change their structure once the cells are removed
The cellular level, because isolated cells have more mitochondria available
The tissue level, because cardiac muscle contracts more slowly when it is attached to valves
cards.explanation: The isolated cells show their intrinsic rate, and the intact resting heart is slower because parasympathetic fibers from the nervous system continuously inhibit the node, a control that only exists when the systems are connected. The channels themselves are unchanged by dissection, so the molecular option fails. Mitochondrial number does not set pacemaker rate. Valves do not slow the electrical rhythm of cardiac muscle.

cards.q: A single amino acid substitution in the beta globin gene changes hemoglobin so it polymerizes at low PO2, and the patient reports pain during exertion. Which statement correctly links the levels?
cards.a: The defect begins at the molecular level and the pain is best explained at the tissue and organ level.
options: Both the defect and the pain are best explained at the molecular level
The defect begins at the molecular level and the pain is best explained at the tissue and organ level
The defect begins at the cellular level and the pain is a molecular event
The defect and the pain both belong to the organ system level because blood is involved
cards.explanation: A changed amino acid is a molecular event, but pain arises because rigid cells block small vessels and starve tissue of oxygen, which is a tissue and organ consequence. Saying both are molecular skips the steps that actually produce the symptom. The defect is not cellular in origin, since the cell shape change follows from the protein change. Calling both organ system level ignores where the original lesion sits.

cards.q: A drug blocks a sodium channel found only in nerve membranes, and a patient given the drug loses sensation in one area of skin. Which sequence of levels correctly traces the effect?
cards.a: Molecular block, then cellular loss of action potentials, then organ system loss of sensation.
options: Molecular block, then cellular loss of action potentials, then organ system loss of sensation
Cellular block, then molecular loss of action potentials, then tissue loss of sensation
Organ block, then tissue loss of action potentials, then molecular loss of sensation
Tissue block, then organ loss of action potentials, then cellular loss of sensation
cards.explanation: The drug binds a protein, so the first step is molecular; without those channels the neuron cannot fire, which is cellular; and sensation is a nervous system function, so the reported symptom sits at the organ system level. The other sequences reverse the order or place action potentials at levels above the single cell that generates them. Effects generally travel upward from the level where the agent acts.

cards.q: A team fully describes the kinetics of every enzyme in a liver cell but still cannot predict how the whole liver responds to a meal. What is the best explanation?
cards.a: Higher levels of organization have emergent properties that come from interactions, not from the parts alone.
options: The enzyme measurements must contain errors, since complete molecular data always predicts organ function
Enzymes stop working at the organ level and other proteins take over the same reactions
Liver function is anatomical rather than physiological, so enzymes are irrelevant to it
Higher levels of organization have emergent properties that come from interactions, not from the parts alone
cards.explanation: Function at a higher level depends on how the parts interact, including blood flow, hormonal signals, and cell to cell communication, so a complete parts list still leaves the assembled behavior unexplained. Assuming measurement error misses the real limit of reductionism. Liver function is very much physiological. Enzymes keep working at every level, so the claim that other proteins take over at the organ level contradicts basic biochemistry.

cards.q: Why is the wall between an alveolus and a pulmonary capillary extremely thin?
cards.a: A short diffusion distance speeds gas exchange.
options: A thin wall increases the resistance of the airway
A thin wall lets alveoli store more air
A short diffusion distance speeds gas exchange
A thin wall keeps blood from entering the capillary
cards.explanation: Diffusion rate falls as the distance the gas must cross rises, so a barrier only a fraction of a micrometer thick lets oxygen and carbon dioxide move quickly between air and blood. Air volume is set by alveolar size, not wall thickness. Airway resistance is a property of the conducting tubes, not the exchange surface. Blood must enter the capillary for exchange to happen at all.

cards.q: What functional advantage does the biconcave disc shape of a red blood cell provide?
cards.a: More surface area for its volume and enough flexibility to bend through capillaries.
options: A place to store extra hemoglobin in the center
More surface area for its volume and enough flexibility to bend through capillaries
Space for a nucleus that directs protein synthesis
A rigid frame that keeps the cell from deforming in vessels
cards.explanation: The dimpled disc raises surface area relative to volume, which shortens the diffusion path for oxygen, and it lets the cell fold to pass through capillaries narrower than the cell itself. Hemoglobin fills the whole cell rather than a central store. Mature human red cells have no nucleus. Rigidity would be a disadvantage, since a stiff cell plugs capillaries.

cards.q: What is the functional role of microvilli on the apical membrane of an intestinal epithelial cell?
cards.a: They increase the surface area available for absorption.
options: They propel material along the surface by beating
They increase the surface area available for absorption
They anchor the cell to the basement membrane
They secrete mucus onto the intestinal surface
cards.explanation: Microvilli are tiny fingerlike folds of membrane that multiply absorptive surface many times over without lengthening the intestine. Beating projections that move material along a surface are cilia, which are longer and motile. Anchoring to the basement membrane is done by junctional and adhesion proteins on the basal side. Mucus comes from goblet cells, a different cell type.

cards.q: How does myelin around an axon change the way that axon functions?
cards.a: It speeds conduction by forcing the signal to jump between nodes.
options: It speeds conduction by forcing the signal to jump between nodes
It increases the number of neurotransmitter molecules released
It allows the axon to conduct signals in both directions at once
It raises the resting membrane potential to zero
cards.explanation: Myelin insulates the membrane so current flows down the axon interior and regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier, which makes conduction much faster than in an unmyelinated fiber of the same diameter. Transmitter release depends on the terminal and its calcium channels, not on the myelin. Direction of travel is set by where the action potential starts. Myelin does not abolish the resting potential.

cards.q: In a skeletal muscle sarcomere, what structural feature determines how much force the fiber can generate at a given length?
cards.a: The amount of overlap between thick and thin filaments.
options: The number of mitochondria packed between the fibers
The thickness of the connective tissue around the whole muscle
The amount of overlap between thick and thin filaments
The length of the tendon attaching the muscle to bone
cards.explanation: Force comes from myosin heads binding actin, so the number of possible cross bridges, and therefore the overlap between the filaments, sets the force at any sarcomere length. Mitochondria supply ATP and affect fatigue resistance rather than peak force per cross bridge. Connective tissue and tendon transmit force but do not generate it.

cards.q: A capillary wall is a single layer of endothelial cells. What does that structure make possible?
cards.a: Rapid exchange of water and small solutes between blood and interstitial fluid.
options: Rapid exchange of water and small solutes between blood and interstitial fluid
Strong contraction that pushes blood forward
Storage of a large reserve volume of blood
Withstanding the highest pressures in the circulation
cards.explanation: With no muscle or thick connective layer in the way, solutes and water cross the capillary wall easily, which is the entire purpose of that vessel. Contraction that propels blood is the job of the heart and, to a small degree, arteriolar smooth muscle. Blood is stored mainly in veins, which are thin walled but large in volume. High pressure is handled by the elastic, muscular walls of arteries.

cards.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
cards.a: It must generate the much higher pressure needed to drive blood through the systemic circuit.
options: It holds a much larger volume of blood than the right ventricle
It receives blood directly from the venae cavae
It contracts more times per minute than the right ventricle
It must generate the much higher pressure needed to drive blood through the systemic circuit
cards.explanation: Systemic resistance is far higher than pulmonary resistance, so the left ventricle needs more muscle to develop the pressure that moves the same stroke volume into the aorta. The two ventricles eject nearly equal volumes over time, so volume is not the reason. Both ventricles beat at the same rate because they are driven by the same conduction system. The venae cavae empty into the right atrium.

cards.q: What structural feature of an enzyme determines which substrate it will act on?
cards.a: The shape and chemistry of its active site.
options: The shape and chemistry of its active site
Its total molecular weight
The number of peptide bonds it contains
The temperature at which it was synthesized
cards.explanation: Substrate specificity comes from a pocket whose shape, charge, and hydrogen bonding partners fit one molecule and exclude others, which is the clearest molecular example of structure setting function. Molecular weight and the count of peptide bonds describe size, and many enzymes of similar size act on completely different substrates. Synthesis temperature does not define the folded binding site.

cards.q: Pulmonary fibrosis thickens the wall between alveolus and capillary. What happens to the rate of oxygen diffusion into blood?
cards.a: It falls, because diffusion rate drops as the distance increases.
options: It rises, because thicker tissue holds more oxygen
It is unchanged, because oxygen is carried by hemoglobin
It falls, because diffusion rate drops as the distance increases
It rises, because thicker walls raise the pressure gradient
cards.explanation: Diffusion is inversely related to the thickness of the barrier, so adding tissue slows oxygen entry and can leave the blood incompletely saturated during exercise. Tissue does not act as an oxygen reservoir that helps loading. Hemoglobin only carries oxygen that has already crossed the barrier. Wall thickness does not change the difference in PO2 between alveolar gas and blood.

cards.q: In celiac disease the intestinal villi flatten and microvilli are lost. What is the predicted functional consequence?
cards.a: Reduced absorption of nutrients because surface area is lost.
options: Reduced absorption of nutrients because surface area is lost
Increased absorption because the surface is now smoother
No change in absorption because transporters are unaffected
Increased motility that compensates fully for the lost surface
cards.explanation: Absorption rate is proportional to the available surface, so flattening the villi removes most of the membrane that carries transporters and slows uptake of sugars, amino acids, and fats. A smooth surface offers less area, not more. Transporters live on the lost membrane, so they are directly reduced. Faster motility would shorten contact time and make absorption worse, not better.

cards.q: A disease strips myelin from peripheral motor axons. What happens to conduction velocity and the strength of muscle activation?
cards.a: Conduction slows and muscle activation weakens.
options: Conduction slows and muscle activation weakens
Conduction speeds up and muscle activation strengthens
Conduction slows but muscle activation is unchanged
Conduction is unchanged but muscle activation weakens
cards.explanation: Without myelin the action potential must be regenerated continuously along the membrane, which slows it and can cause the signal to fail before it reaches the terminal, so fewer fibers are recruited on time and force drops. Demyelination never speeds conduction, since the insulation is what allows the jump between nodes. Slowing and failure occur together, so muscle activation cannot stay normal, and conduction cannot be normal while the axon is bare.

cards.q: Chronic hypertension makes the left ventricular wall thick and stiff. What does this structural change do to ventricular filling during diastole?
cards.a: Filling is reduced because a stiffer chamber accepts less volume for a given pressure.
options: Filling improves because a thicker wall relaxes faster
Filling improves because the chamber volume increases
Filling is unchanged because diastole is a passive process
Filling is reduced because a stiffer chamber accepts less volume for a given pressure
cards.explanation: Compliance is volume gained per unit of filling pressure, and stiff muscle lowers compliance, so the ventricle takes in less blood even when atrial pressure rises. Thicker muscle relaxes more slowly, not faster. Diastole being passive is exactly why chamber stiffness matters so much. Wall thickening usually shrinks the chamber cavity rather than enlarging it.

cards.q: An arteriole constricts so that its radius is halved. Given that resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius, resistance in that vessel becomes about how many times greater?
cards.a: Sixteen times greater.
options: Two times greater
Four times greater
Sixteen times greater
Eight times greater
cards.explanation: Halving the radius means multiplying resistance by two raised to the fourth power, which is sixteen, so small changes in arteriolar diameter produce very large changes in flow. Two times would apply if resistance varied directly with radius. Four times would apply to a squared relationship, and eight times to a cubed one. The fourth power dependence is what makes arterioles the main control point for blood flow.

cards.q: A point mutation changes an amino acid inside the active site of a metabolic enzyme. What is the most likely functional result?
cards.a: The substrate binds poorly and the reaction rate falls.
options: The enzyme now catalyzes a completely unrelated reaction at full speed
The reaction rate rises because the site is now more open
The enzyme is destroyed immediately because any mutation is lethal to a protein
The substrate binds poorly and the reaction rate falls
cards.explanation: Catalysis depends on precise contact between the substrate and the residues lining the pocket, so altering one of those residues usually weakens binding and slows the reaction. Acquiring a brand new efficient activity from a single substitution is extremely unlikely. Many mutations are tolerated, so the protein is not automatically destroyed. A looser pocket generally holds the substrate less well rather than working faster.

cards.q: Inflammation widens the gaps between capillary endothelial cells. What is the predicted effect on the interstitial fluid?
cards.a: Protein and fluid leak out of the capillary and interstitial volume rises.
options: Interstitial volume falls because plasma proteins are retained
Only red blood cells cross, so interstitial protein is unchanged
Protein and fluid leak out of the capillary and interstitial volume rises
Water is pulled back into the capillary because the gaps raise blood pressure
cards.explanation: Wider clefts let plasma proteins escape, which raises interstitial oncotic pressure and drags water with them, producing the swelling of inflamed tissue. Retaining protein is what an intact capillary does, and that is the situation being lost here. Red cells are far too large to be the main species crossing widened clefts. Leakiness does not raise capillary hydrostatic pressure.

cards.q: In emphysema, the walls between alveoli break down so many small alveoli merge into fewer large ones. Trace the consequence for gas exchange.
cards.a: Total surface area falls, so oxygen transfer per breath drops and arterial PO2 falls.
options: Surface area is unchanged because the same volume of air is present
Total surface area rises because the spaces are larger, so arterial PO2 rises
Diffusion distance falls because the walls are gone, so arterial PO2 rises
Total surface area falls, so oxygen transfer per breath drops and arterial PO2 falls
cards.explanation: Many small spheres have far more combined surface than a few large ones of the same total volume, so destroying septa removes exchange surface and less oxygen enters the blood per breath. Larger air spaces feel roomier but offer less membrane, so calling the surface area increased confuses volume with area. Losing walls also removes the capillaries embedded in them, so there is no benefit from a shorter path. Equal air volume does not mean equal surface.

cards.q: Sickled red blood cells are rigid rather than flexible. Follow the chain of consequences in a small capillary bed.
cards.a: The rigid cells cannot deform to pass, flow is obstructed, and the tissue downstream becomes hypoxic.
options: The rigid cells carry more oxygen, so downstream tissue is better supplied
The rigid cells widen the capillary permanently, so flow increases
The rigid cells cannot deform to pass, flow is obstructed, and the tissue downstream becomes hypoxic
The rigid cells pass unchanged because capillary diameter always exceeds cell diameter
cards.explanation: A normal red cell folds to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself, and losing that flexibility turns the cell into a plug, so blood flow stops and the tissue beyond it runs short of oxygen. Rigidity does not increase oxygen carriage, and sickled cells actually release oxygen readily. Capillaries are not permanently widened by an obstructing cell. Many capillaries are narrower than a red cell, which is exactly why deformability matters.

cards.q: Damage to the filtration slits of glomerular podocytes lets plasma albumin escape into the urine. Predict the effect on fluid distribution in the body.
cards.a: Plasma oncotic pressure falls, so less fluid is reabsorbed into capillaries and edema develops.
options: Plasma oncotic pressure rises, so fluid is pulled out of tissues and edema resolves
Nothing changes in the tissues because albumin acts only inside the kidney
Plasma volume rises because losing protein draws water into the vessels
Plasma oncotic pressure falls, so less fluid is reabsorbed into capillaries and edema develops
cards.explanation: Albumin is the main protein holding water inside systemic capillaries, so losing it into urine lowers plasma oncotic pressure and tips the balance at every capillary toward net filtration, which shows up as swelling. Oncotic pressure cannot rise while protein is being lost. Water follows protein, so losing protein from plasma pulls water out of vessels rather than in. This case links the renal and cardiovascular systems, which is why the effect is body wide.

cards.q: An athlete trains for endurance and the capillary density in the trained muscle increases. What functional change follows, and why?
cards.a: Oxygen delivery improves because diffusion distance to each fiber falls and exchange surface rises.
options: Oxygen delivery falls because more capillaries slow blood flow through the muscle
Oxygen delivery improves because diffusion distance to each fiber falls and exchange surface rises
Peak force rises because capillaries generate tension alongside the fibers
Nothing changes because oxygen delivery is set entirely by hemoglobin concentration
cards.explanation: More capillaries per fiber means each muscle cell sits closer to a source of oxygen and the total exchange surface is larger, so more oxygen can be delivered during sustained work. Extra parallel channels lower resistance and raise flow rather than slowing it. Capillaries have no contractile filaments, so they add no force. Hemoglobin sets carrying capacity, but delivery also depends on how easily oxygen reaches the fiber.

cards.q: What does homeostasis mean?
cards.a: Active maintenance of the internal environment within a narrow range compatible with life.
options: Keeping every internal variable at exactly one fixed number
The state in which forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates
Active maintenance of the internal environment within a narrow range compatible with life
The tendency of body fluids to match the composition of the outside world
cards.explanation: Homeostasis is regulation, meaning the body senses deviations and acts to bring a variable back into an acceptable range, which is why the range matters more than a single number. Perfect constancy never occurs, since regulated variables oscillate around their setpoints. Equal forward and reverse rates describe chemical equilibrium, which is a different idea. Matching the outside world would abolish the gradients life depends on.

cards.q: What is a regulated variable?
cards.a: A quantity the body monitors and actively holds within a narrow range.
options: Any quantity that changes during the day
A quantity the body monitors and actively holds within a narrow range
A quantity that is altered in order to hold something else constant
A quantity that cannot be measured in the clinic
cards.explanation: A regulated variable such as core temperature, plasma osmolarity, or mean arterial pressure is sensed by receptors and defended by reflexes. Many quantities change during the day without being defended, so mere variation is not the test. A quantity that is changed in order to protect something else is a controlled variable, such as heart rate serving blood pressure. Measurability in the clinic has nothing to do with whether the body regulates it.

cards.q: What is a setpoint?
cards.a: The value of a regulated variable that the control system defends.
options: The highest value a variable can reach before damage occurs
The average of all measurements taken over one day
The point at which a reflex pathway crosses the spinal cord
The value of a regulated variable that the control system defends
cards.explanation: The setpoint is the target the integrating center compares incoming information against, and any deviation from it drives a corrective response. The upper limit before damage is a tolerance, not a target. Where a reflex crosses the cord is anatomy of the pathway. A daily average may sit near the setpoint but it is a description of data rather than the value being defended.

cards.q: What defines chemical equilibrium?
cards.a: No net movement or net reaction, and no energy input required to hold the state.
options: Concentrations stay constant only because a pump keeps working
A sensor detects a change and corrects it continuously
Concentrations on both sides of a membrane are always equal in number
No net movement or net reaction, and no energy input required to hold the state
cards.explanation: At equilibrium the system has run down to its lowest free energy state, so nothing further needs to be spent to keep it there. A state that depends on a working pump is a steady state, which is the key contrast for this course. Equal concentrations are not required at equilibrium when charge or pressure differences balance the chemical difference. Sensing and correcting describes homeostatic regulation, not equilibrium.

cards.q: What defines a steady state?
cards.a: A constant value maintained by continuous input of energy, with material still moving.
options: A constant value maintained by continuous input of energy, with material still moving
A constant value reached after all net movement has stopped
A value that changes predictably with the time of day
A value that is identical in every body fluid compartment
cards.explanation: In a steady state, what enters equals what leaves, so the amount stays constant while flow continues, and holding that flow costs energy. Once all net movement stops the system is at equilibrium, not steady state. A predictable daily rhythm describes a circadian pattern. Identical values everywhere would mean gradients have collapsed.

cards.q: Which of these is a regulated variable rather than a variable changed in order to defend something else?
cards.a: Mean arterial pressure.
options: Heart rate
Mean arterial pressure
Sweat rate
Vessel diameter
cards.explanation: Mean arterial pressure is sensed by baroreceptors and defended by reflexes, so it is the quantity the system protects. Heart rate and vessel diameter are the outputs adjusted in order to hold pressure steady, which makes them controlled variables. Sweat rate is likewise an output adjusted to defend core temperature.

cards.q: When physiologists say homeostasis maintains the internal environment, which fluid are they mainly referring to?
cards.a: Extracellular fluid.
options: Intracellular fluid
Extracellular fluid
Fluid inside the digestive tract
Fluid in the urinary bladder
cards.explanation: Cells are bathed in extracellular fluid, so keeping its composition stable is what protects every cell in the body, and that fluid is what reflexes actually defend. Intracellular fluid composition varies with cell type and is defended cell by cell rather than by whole body reflexes. The digestive tract and the bladder are continuous with the outside world, so their contents are not part of the internal environment.

cards.q: How does a normal range differ from a setpoint?
cards.a: The normal range is the band of values found in healthy people, while the setpoint is the single value the system defends.
options: They are two names for the same number
The setpoint is always the midpoint of the normal range in every person
The normal range applies to one person and the setpoint applies to a population
The normal range is the band of values found in healthy people, while the setpoint is the single value the system defends
cards.explanation: A normal range is a statistical description of healthy values, while a setpoint is a property of one person's control system at one time and can be reset, as it is in fever. The two are not synonyms, since a range has width and a setpoint does not. Assigning the range to one person and the setpoint to a population reverses the two. An individual setpoint need not land exactly at the middle of the published range.

cards.q: A living cell keeps intracellular Na+ near 12 mEq/L while extracellular Na+ stays near 140 mEq/L, and the concentrations do not change over hours. Is this equilibrium or steady state?
cards.a: Steady state, because the pump must keep spending ATP to hold the gradient.
options: Steady state, because the pump must keep spending ATP to hold the gradient
Equilibrium, because the concentrations are not changing
Equilibrium, because sodium leaks in and is pumped out at equal rates
Neither, because a stable gradient is not a defined physiological state
cards.explanation: Constant concentrations plus continuous energy expenditure is the definition of a steady state, and here the Na+ that leaks in is pumped back out at the same rate. Unchanging numbers alone do not prove equilibrium, which is the exact confusion this card targets. Equal leak and pump rates describe balance in a steady state, not equilibrium, because a pump is doing work. Stable gradients are very much a defined state.

cards.q: A sealed flask holds a saturated salt solution with solid salt at the bottom, and the dissolved concentration no longer changes. Which state is this?
cards.a: Chemical equilibrium, because no energy is required to maintain it.
options: Homeostasis, because the concentration is stable
Steady state, because dissolving and crystallizing both continue
Chemical equilibrium, because no energy is required to maintain it
A regulated variable, because the concentration has a setpoint
cards.explanation: Dissolution and crystallization occur at equal rates with no outside energy supplied, which is the textbook picture of equilibrium. Homeostasis requires sensors and effectors that this flask does not have. Steady state is reserved for systems that need continuous energy input to stay constant, which this one does not. Nothing in the flask sets or defends a target value.

cards.q: During a run, core temperature stays near 37 C while sweat rate climbs sharply. Which variable is regulated?
cards.a: Core temperature, with sweat rate serving as the controlled output.
options: Sweat rate, with core temperature serving as the controlled output
Neither is regulated, since both changed during exercise
Both are regulated variables with separate setpoints
Core temperature, with sweat rate serving as the controlled output
cards.explanation: The variable held steady while other things change is the one being defended, so core temperature is regulated and sweating is the effector response that defends it. Reversing the two mistakes the tool for the goal. Sweat rate has no setpoint of its own; it simply follows the thermal error signal. Core temperature stayed close to normal, which is evidence that regulation succeeded rather than failed.

cards.q: An infection raises the thermal setpoint in the hypothalamus from 37 C to 39 C. What does the person feel and do at a body temperature of 37 C?
cards.a: They feel cold and shiver, because the body reads 37 C as too low.
options: They feel hot and sweat, because the body reads 37 C as too high
They feel cold and shiver, because the body reads 37 C as too low
They feel nothing unusual, because 37 C is the normal value
They sweat and shiver at the same time to reach the new value faster
cards.explanation: The control system compares actual temperature against the current setpoint, so once the target moves to 39 C an actual value of 37 C is an error in the cold direction and triggers heat gaining responses. Sweating happens later, when the fever breaks and the setpoint returns to normal, leaving actual temperature too high. Comfort at 37 C would require the setpoint to still be 37 C. Shivering and sweating oppose each other and are not activated together.

cards.q: Blood glucose rises from 90 to 140 mg/dL after a meal and returns to 95 mg/dL two hours later. What does this pattern show?
cards.a: Homeostasis working, since the regulated variable was returned to its range.
options: Chemical equilibrium, since the value ended where it started
Homeostasis working, since the regulated variable was returned to its range
A failure of homeostasis, since the value left 90 at all
A steady state, since glucose did not change during the meal
cards.explanation: Homeostasis does not prevent all change; it detects a deviation and corrects it, which is exactly the pattern described. A return to the starting value does not make it equilibrium, since insulin secretion and glucose uptake required energy and active signaling. Brief excursions outside the resting value are normal and expected after eating. Glucose clearly did change during the meal, so calling this a steady state contradicts the data.

cards.q: If a cell completely stopped producing ATP, what would happen to the ion gradients across its membrane?
cards.a: They would dissipate until the ions reached equilibrium.
options: They would dissipate until the ions reached equilibrium
They would become steeper as ions stopped moving
They would be held by the membrane, which blocks all ion movement
They would reverse, putting Na+ inside and K+ outside at high concentration
cards.explanation: Gradients are a steady state paid for by the Na+ K+ ATPase, so removing ATP lets leak channels carry ions down their gradients until net movement stops, which is equilibrium and is also cell death. Gradients cannot steepen without a pump doing work. The membrane leaks ions continuously through channels, so it is not an absolute barrier. Nothing would drive an active reversal once the energy supply is gone.

cards.q: Which described situation requires continuous energy input to stay constant?
cards.a: Plasma calcium held near 10 mg/dL while calcium moves between bone, gut, and urine.
options: Plasma calcium held near 10 mg/dL while calcium moves between bone, gut, and urine
Oxygen and nitrogen concentrations in a sealed tank of air
The pH of a buffer solution sitting on a bench
The salt concentration of seawater in a closed jar
cards.explanation: Plasma calcium is constant only because hormones drive absorption, bone exchange, and renal handling, and every one of those transport steps costs energy. The sealed tank, the bench buffer, and the closed jar are all at equilibrium and stay constant with nothing being spent. Recognizing the cost of stability is what separates steady state from equilibrium.

cards.q: A cell in a dish is treated with a drug that fully blocks the Na+ K+ ATPase. Describe how the cell moves between states over the next hour.
cards.a: It leaves steady state, drifts as ions redistribute, and approaches equilibrium with the bath.
options: It moves from equilibrium into a new steady state with a steeper gradient
It stays in steady state because leak channels alone can maintain the gradient
It leaves steady state, drifts as ions redistribute, and approaches equilibrium with the bath
It reaches homeostasis because the concentrations eventually stop changing
cards.explanation: The gradients existed only because the pump kept working against the leaks, so blocking the pump lets Na+ enter and K+ leave until net movement ceases, which is equilibrium and not a survivable state. Steady state cannot become steeper without energy, so a steeper gradient after the pump is blocked reverses the direction. Leak channels dissipate gradients rather than build them. Constancy at equilibrium is not homeostasis, because no sensor or effector is defending anything.

cards.q: A patient with advanced kidney disease has a plasma K+ of 5.8 mEq/L that has been stable at that value for months, with intake equal to output. How should this be described?
cards.a: A steady state that lies outside the homeostatic range for K+.
options: Normal homeostasis, because the value is stable over months
A steady state that lies outside the homeostatic range for K+
Chemical equilibrium, because intake and output are equal
A change in the K+ setpoint to 5.8 mEq/L
cards.explanation: Intake matching output keeps the amount constant, which is a steady state, but the defended value has been overwhelmed and the plasma level sits above the healthy range, so stability here is not health. Calling it normal homeostasis ignores that the regulated variable is out of range. Equilibrium would require no energy expenditure, and renal and cellular transport are still working hard. The setpoint has not moved; the system simply cannot reach it.

cards.q: A person eats 2800 kcal a day, exercises heavily, and keeps a constant body weight for a year. A rock sitting in a field also keeps a constant weight. Which comparison is correct?
cards.a: The person is in a steady state and the rock is at equilibrium.
options: Both are in a steady state, since neither weight is changing
The person is at equilibrium and the rock is in a steady state
Both are at equilibrium, since input equals output in each case
The person is in a steady state and the rock is at equilibrium
cards.explanation: The person holds constant mass only because large flows of energy and matter in and out are balanced, which costs energy continuously, while the rock is simply at rest with nothing flowing. Calling both steady states ignores that the rock spends nothing. The rock has no meaningful input or output to balance. Calling the person equilibrated and the rock a steady state reverses the two cases.

cards.q: Plasma osmolarity is defended near 290 mOsm/L, and after a person drinks a liter of water it falls to 283 mOsm/L and is back to 289 mOsm/L within two hours. Which statement best interprets the sequence?
cards.a: Osmolarity is the regulated variable, urine output is the controlled response, and the correction shows negative feedback.
options: Urine output is the regulated variable and osmolarity is the controlled response
The return to 289 mOsm/L shows the body reached chemical equilibrium with the water
The dip to 283 mOsm/L proves that osmolarity is not regulated at all
Osmolarity is the regulated variable, urine output is the controlled response, and the correction shows negative feedback
cards.explanation: Osmoreceptors sensed the fall, antidiuretic hormone secretion dropped, and dilute urine was produced until osmolarity came back toward the setpoint, which is the classic shape of a negative feedback correction. Urine volume is the output adjusted to protect osmolarity, not the defended variable. A transient deviation that is corrected is evidence of regulation, not evidence against it. Equilibrium would mean no energy spent, but renal transport ran the entire time.

cards.q: What is the job of the sensor in a negative feedback loop?
cards.a: To detect the value of the regulated variable and report it.
options: To compare the value against the setpoint
To detect the value of the regulated variable and report it
To carry out the corrective action
To carry the command signal to the tissue
cards.explanation: A sensor, such as a thermoreceptor or a baroreceptor, measures the variable and converts that measurement into a signal the body can transmit. Comparison against the setpoint happens later, in the integrating center. Carrying out the correction is the effector's role, and carrying the command is the efferent path.

cards.q: What does the integrating center do?
cards.a: It compares the incoming information with the setpoint and decides on a response.
options: It converts a stimulus into an electrical signal
It changes the value of the regulated variable directly
It compares the incoming information with the setpoint and decides on a response
It transports the corrective signal to distant tissues
cards.explanation: The integrating center holds the setpoint, evaluates the error between the actual and target value, and issues an output proportional to that error. Converting a stimulus into a signal is transduction by the sensor. Changing the variable is the effector's action. Transporting the signal is the efferent pathway, whether it is a nerve or the bloodstream.

cards.q: In which direction does the afferent pathway carry information?
cards.a: From the sensor to the integrating center.
options: From the sensor to the integrating center
From the integrating center to the effector
From the effector back to the stimulus
From the integrating center to the sensor
cards.explanation: Afferent means carrying toward the center, so this limb brings the measurement inward for comparison with the setpoint. Carrying from the center out to the effector is the efferent limb, and confusing these two is the most common error in this topic. Effectors do not signal back to the stimulus directly, and the center does not send instructions to the sensor.

cards.q: What does the efferent pathway carry?
cards.a: The command signal from the integrating center to the effector.
options: The setpoint value to the sensor
Sensory information from the receptor inward
The command signal from the integrating center to the effector
The regulated variable itself to the effector
cards.explanation: Efferent means carrying away from the center, and this limb may be a motor nerve or a hormone in the blood. Sensory information travelling inward is the afferent limb. The setpoint stays inside the integrating center and is never shipped to the sensor. A pathway carries signals, not the regulated variable itself.

cards.q: What is an effector?
cards.a: The cell, tissue, or organ that carries out the response.
options: The structure that holds the setpoint
The signal molecule that travels in the blood
The change in the regulated variable that starts the loop
The cell, tissue, or organ that carries out the response
cards.explanation: Sweat glands, skeletal muscle, the heart, and the liver all act as effectors when they change their activity to correct a deviation. Holding the setpoint is the integrating center's role. A signal molecule in the blood is part of the efferent pathway. The change that starts the loop is the stimulus.

cards.q: Which structure serves as the integrating center for body temperature regulation?
cards.a: The hypothalamus.
options: The cerebellum
The medulla oblongata
The hypothalamus
The anterior pituitary
cards.explanation: The hypothalamus holds the thermal setpoint, receives input from central and skin thermoreceptors, and drives shivering, sweating, and skin blood flow. The cerebellum coordinates movement rather than temperature. The medulla is the integrating center for cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes. The anterior pituitary secretes hormones on command from the hypothalamus, so it is downstream rather than the comparator.

cards.q: Where are the sensors that report skin temperature to the thermoregulatory loop?
cards.a: Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin.
options: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
Chemoreceptors in the aortic body
Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin
cards.explanation: Skin thermoreceptors sense the temperature of the body surface and send that information to the hypothalamus, giving early warning before core temperature itself changes. Baroreceptors report arterial stretch and therefore pressure. Aortic chemoreceptors report oxygen and carbon dioxide levels. Osmoreceptors report plasma osmolarity, a different regulated variable.

cards.q: In the loop that regulates blood glucose after a meal, which cell acts as the sensor?
cards.a: The pancreatic beta cell.
options: The pancreatic beta cell
The hepatocyte
The skeletal muscle fiber
The adipocyte
cards.explanation: The beta cell takes up glucose in proportion to plasma glucose and secretes insulin accordingly, so it both senses and compares. Hepatocytes, muscle fibers, and adipocytes all respond to insulin, which makes them effectors in this loop rather than sensors.

cards.q: A person becomes overheated and sweat glands begin to secrete. Which loop component are the sweat glands?
cards.a: The effector.
options: The effector
The afferent pathway
The sensor
The integrating center
cards.explanation: Sweat glands perform the action that removes heat, which is the definition of an effector. Sensors detect temperature and do not act on it. The afferent pathway carries information inward. The integrating center for this loop is the hypothalamus, not the gland.

cards.q: Insulin released by the pancreas travels in the blood to the liver and muscle. Which component of the feedback loop is that travel?
cards.a: The efferent pathway.
options: The afferent pathway
The stimulus
The response
The efferent pathway
cards.explanation: The efferent limb carries the command from the integrating center to the effectors, and a hormone in the bloodstream does exactly that job. The afferent limb would carry information toward the center instead. The stimulus was the rise in glucose. The response is the fall in glucose that follows insulin action.

cards.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 90 to 140 mg/dL. In the glucose feedback loop, what is that rise?
cards.a: The stimulus.
options: The stimulus
The response
The effector output
The setpoint
cards.explanation: The stimulus is the change in the regulated variable that starts the loop, and here it is the postprandial rise in glucose. The response is the later fall back toward normal. Effector output would be glucose uptake and storage by liver and muscle. The setpoint is the target value the system defends, not the deviation itself.

cards.q: A sensory neuron carries impulses from a cold thermoreceptor in the skin up to the hypothalamus. Which component is this neuron?
cards.a: The afferent pathway.
options: The efferent pathway
The afferent pathway
The integrating center
The effector
cards.explanation: Information travelling from a receptor toward the comparator is the afferent limb, and this is the classic place students reverse the terms. The efferent limb would run from the hypothalamus out to skin blood vessels or to skeletal muscle. The integrating center is the hypothalamus itself, and the effectors are the vessels and muscles that respond.

cards.q: Two hours after a meal, blood glucose has come back down to 92 mg/dL. Which component of the loop is that fall?
cards.a: The response.
options: The stimulus
The afferent signal
The response
The sensor output
cards.explanation: The response is the change in the regulated variable produced by the effectors, and it is what shuts the loop down as the error shrinks. The stimulus was the earlier rise in glucose. The afferent signal in this loop is insulin secretion driven by beta cell sensing, which occurs before the fall. Sensor output reports the value rather than being the value.

cards.q: An injury damages the hypothalamus so that body temperature is no longer defended, although skin receptors, nerves, sweat glands, and muscles all work normally. Which component has been lost?
cards.a: The integrating center.
options: The integrating center
The sensor
The effector
The afferent pathway
cards.explanation: Every other part of the loop is intact, so the failure must sit at the comparison step where the setpoint lives, which is the hypothalamus. Intact skin receptors rule out sensor loss. Working sweat glands and muscles rule out effector failure. Intact nerves carrying information inward rule out an afferent lesion.

cards.q: In the insulin loop, what is unusual about the beta cell compared with the thermoregulatory loop?
cards.a: The beta cell serves as sensor and integrating center in one cell.
options: The loop has no efferent pathway because insulin is a hormone
The beta cell is the effector and has no sensing role
The beta cell serves as sensor and integrating center in one cell
The loop has no setpoint because glucose is not regulated
cards.explanation: The beta cell measures glucose and adjusts insulin output itself, so the sensing and comparing steps collapse into one cell with no separate afferent nerve. The effectors are the liver, muscle, and fat cells that take up glucose. Insulin travelling in blood is a perfectly good efferent pathway, since efferent limbs can be neural or hormonal. Glucose is one of the most tightly regulated variables in the body.

cards.q: A person steps into cold air and begins to shiver. Which order correctly traces the loop?
cards.a: Cold stimulus, skin thermoreceptors, sensory nerves, hypothalamus, motor nerves, skeletal muscle, heat production.
options: Cold stimulus, hypothalamus, skin thermoreceptors, motor nerves, sensory nerves, skeletal muscle, heat production
Cold stimulus, skin thermoreceptors, sensory nerves, hypothalamus, motor nerves, skeletal muscle, heat production
Cold stimulus, skeletal muscle, motor nerves, hypothalamus, sensory nerves, skin thermoreceptors, heat production
Cold stimulus, sensory nerves, skin thermoreceptors, motor nerves, hypothalamus, skeletal muscle, heat production
cards.explanation: Information must be detected before it can be sent, compared before a command is issued, and delivered before an effector acts, which gives the sequence stimulus, sensor, afferent, center, efferent, effector, response. One wrong sequence places the hypothalamus before the receptors have detected anything, another runs the loop backward by starting at skeletal muscle, and a third puts the sensory nerve ahead of the receptor it comes from while swapping the center with the efferent limb.

cards.q: Trace the blood glucose loop after a carbohydrate meal. Which sequence is correct?
cards.a: Glucose rises, beta cell senses and compares, insulin travels in blood, liver and muscle take up glucose, glucose falls.
options: Glucose rises, liver releases glucose, insulin is secreted, beta cell senses the change, glucose falls
Insulin is secreted, glucose rises, beta cell senses the change, muscle releases glucose, glucose falls
Glucose rises, beta cell senses and compares, insulin travels in blood, liver and muscle take up glucose, glucose falls
Glucose rises, glucagon travels in blood, liver takes up glucose, beta cell senses the change, glucose falls
cards.explanation: The rise is the stimulus, the beta cell is the sensor and comparator, insulin is the efferent signal, the liver and muscle are the effectors, and the fall in glucose is the response that closes the loop. Releasing glucose from the liver would worsen the deviation rather than correct it. Insulin cannot precede the stimulus that causes it. Glucagon is the signal for low glucose, not high.

cards.q: A spinal cord lesion destroys the sensory tracts carrying skin temperature information, while motor pathways to sweat glands and muscle remain intact. What is the predicted defect?
cards.a: The hypothalamus is not warned early about surface cooling, so corrective responses are delayed until core temperature itself changes.
options: Sweating and shivering become impossible even when core temperature changes
Skin blood vessels dilate maximally because the efferent limb has been cut
The thermal setpoint rises and the person runs a permanent fever
The hypothalamus is not warned early about surface cooling, so corrective responses are delayed until core temperature itself changes
cards.explanation: Skin receptors give advance notice of a thermal challenge, so losing that afferent input removes the early warning while central thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus can still detect core changes later. Effector responses remain possible because the motor limb is intact. Cutting an afferent path does not reset the setpoint, so fever is not expected. Maximal dilation would suggest efferent loss, which the question rules out.

cards.q: In type 1 diabetes the pancreatic beta cells are destroyed while liver, muscle, and fat cells still respond normally to insulin given by injection. Which components of the glucose loop are missing?
cards.a: The sensor and integrating center, along with the hormone that forms the efferent signal.
options: The effectors, since the tissues can no longer take up glucose
The setpoint, since glucose is no longer a regulated variable
The stimulus, since blood glucose no longer rises after a meal
The sensor and integrating center, along with the hormone that forms the efferent signal
cards.explanation: The beta cell both senses glucose and issues insulin, so losing it removes the measuring, comparing, and signaling steps at once, which is why injected insulin can replace the signal but cannot restore moment to moment regulation. The effector tissues respond normally to insulin, so they are intact. Glucose still rises after meals, so the stimulus remains. The physiological setpoint has not changed; the loop simply cannot reach it on its own.

cards.q: In negative feedback, how does the response relate to the stimulus?
cards.a: The response moves the variable in the opposite direction from the stimulus.
options: The response moves the variable further in the same direction
The response moves the variable in the opposite direction from the stimulus
The response has no effect on the variable that started the loop
The response changes the setpoint instead of the variable
cards.explanation: Negative feedback opposes change, so a rise triggers a response that lowers the variable and a fall triggers a response that raises it, which is what produces stability. Reinforcing the change is positive feedback. A response with no effect on the variable would not close a loop at all. Moving the setpoint is a separate event, as happens in fever.

cards.q: In positive feedback, how does the response relate to the stimulus?
cards.a: The response amplifies the original change.
options: The response cancels the original change
The response amplifies the original change
The response holds the variable exactly at the setpoint
The response alternates between opposing and amplifying the change
cards.explanation: Positive feedback drives the variable further from where it started, which is useful when the body needs a process to run to completion quickly. Cancelling the change describes negative feedback. Holding a variable at a setpoint is the goal of negative feedback, not positive. No physiological loop alternates between opposing and amplifying its own stimulus.

cards.q: Which process is a classic example of positive feedback in the body?
cards.a: Oxytocin release during labor.
options: Baroreceptor control of blood pressure
Oxytocin release during labor
Insulin release after a meal
Sweating during exercise
cards.explanation: Stretch of the cervix triggers oxytocin, oxytocin strengthens contractions, and stronger contractions stretch the cervix further, so the loop builds on itself. Baroreceptor reflexes, insulin secretion, and sweating all oppose the change that started them, which makes them negative feedback.

cards.q: Which type of feedback dominates in homeostatic regulation?
cards.a: Negative feedback.
options: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward control
Equilibrium feedback
cards.explanation: Almost every regulated variable is defended by loops that oppose deviation, so negative feedback is the general rule and positive feedback the rare exception. Positive feedback is reserved for processes meant to finish quickly, such as labor or clotting. Feedforward is anticipatory and acts before a change occurs, so it is not the mechanism that holds variables steady. Equilibrium feedback is not a physiological term.

cards.q: What ends a positive feedback loop?
cards.a: An event outside the loop that removes the original stimulus.
options: An event outside the loop that removes the original stimulus
The response itself, once it grows large enough
The setpoint automatically resetting to a new value
Fatigue of the sensor after prolonged signaling
cards.explanation: Because the response feeds the stimulus, nothing inside the loop can stop it, so it ends only when something external interrupts it, such as delivery of the infant or sealing of the damaged vessel. A larger response only accelerates the cycle. Positive feedback loops are not organized around a defended setpoint. Sensor fatigue is not a reliable stopping mechanism and is not what the physiology depends on.

cards.q: Blood clotting is described as a positive feedback process. What makes it so?
cards.a: Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors, accelerating the process.
options: Each clotting factor is inhibited by the one before it
Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors, accelerating the process
The clot forms at a constant rate set by a single enzyme
Platelets prevent further platelets from arriving at the injury
cards.explanation: Each activated factor generates more active downstream factors, and platelets that stick release chemicals recruiting more platelets, so the plug builds explosively at the injury site. Serial inhibition would slow rather than amplify. A constant rate would not produce the rapid burst clotting requires. Excluding new platelets would prevent a plug from forming.

cards.q: What pattern does a well functioning negative feedback loop produce in the regulated variable over time?
cards.a: Small oscillations around the setpoint.
options: A steady rise away from the setpoint
A perfectly flat line with no variation at all
Small oscillations around the setpoint
A sudden jump to a new value that is then held
cards.explanation: Because sensing and responding take time, the variable overshoots slightly in each direction, producing gentle swings centered on the setpoint. A steady rise away from the target is the signature of positive feedback or of failed regulation. Perfect flatness is impossible in a loop that must detect an error before correcting it. A jump to a new held value suggests the setpoint itself was reset.

cards.q: Which statement about positive feedback in the body is accurate?
cards.a: It is used for processes that should go to completion quickly.
options: It is always pathological and never appears in health
It is the main mechanism holding plasma osmolarity steady
It is used for processes that should go to completion quickly
It requires a sensor that reports the variable is at its setpoint
cards.explanation: Labor, clotting, and the upstroke of the action potential all benefit from a mechanism that accelerates once started and finishes fast. Positive feedback is normal in these settings, so calling it always pathological is wrong. Osmolarity is defended by negative feedback through antidiuretic hormone and thirst. A setpoint comparison is a feature of negative feedback, not positive.

cards.q: Blood pressure falls, baroreceptors fire less, and heart rate rises to bring pressure back up. Which type of feedback is this?
cards.a: Negative feedback, because the response opposes the fall.
options: Positive feedback, because heart rate rose
Positive feedback, because two variables changed together
Feedforward, because the heart acted before pressure changed
Negative feedback, because the response opposes the fall
cards.explanation: The sign of a loop is judged by whether the response opposes or amplifies the original change, and here a fall in pressure produced a correction that raises pressure. Heart rate rising is the mechanism of the correction, not evidence of amplification. The response came after the pressure fell, so it is not anticipatory. Two variables changing together says nothing about the sign of the loop.

cards.q: During the upstroke of an action potential, sodium entry depolarizes the membrane, which opens more voltage gated sodium channels. Classify this loop.
cards.a: Positive feedback, because the response increases the stimulus.
options: Negative feedback, because the membrane returns to rest afterward
Feedforward, because the cell anticipates the stimulus
Positive feedback, because the response increases the stimulus
Neither, because ion movement is passive
cards.explanation: Depolarization opens channels whose current causes further depolarization, which is why the upstroke is so fast and all or none. The later return to rest is caused by different channels and does not change the sign of the upstroke loop. Nothing about this is anticipatory. Passive ion movement can still form a feedback loop, since the loop is defined by the causal chain rather than by the energy source.

cards.q: Plasma osmolarity rises, antidiuretic hormone is released, the kidney conserves water, and osmolarity falls back toward normal. Classify this loop.
cards.a: Negative feedback.
options: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward control
Acclimatization
cards.explanation: The response lowered the variable that had risen, which is opposition and therefore negative feedback. Positive feedback would have driven osmolarity higher still. Feedforward would act before osmolarity changed, for instance thirst triggered by the taste of salty food. Acclimatization is a slow adaptive change over days, not a single corrective loop.

cards.q: Stretch of the cervix during labor increases oxytocin secretion, which strengthens uterine contractions, which stretches the cervix further. What finally ends this cycle?
cards.a: Delivery of the infant, which removes the stretch stimulus.
options: Delivery of the infant, which removes the stretch stimulus
Oxytocin receptors reaching their maximum firing rate
A negative feedback loop within the uterus that limits contraction
The pituitary running out of stored oxytocin
cards.explanation: Because each turn of the loop increases the stimulus, the cycle can only stop when the stimulus is physically removed, and birth accomplishes that. Receptor saturation would slow the acceleration but would not remove the ongoing stretch. There is no internal opposing loop that halts labor once it is established. Oxytocin supply is not the limiting factor in a normal delivery.

cards.q: A control system is described as having a very low gain, meaning the effector response to a given error is weak. What is the predicted effect on the regulated variable?
cards.a: Larger swings away from the setpoint before correction occurs.
options: Elimination of the setpoint from the integrating center
Perfectly flat control with no deviation at all
Conversion of the loop from negative to positive feedback
Larger swings away from the setpoint before correction occurs
cards.explanation: Gain determines how forcefully the system pushes back per unit of error, so a weak response lets the variable drift further before it is brought under control. Low gain cannot produce tighter control than high gain. The sign of the loop is unchanged, since the response still opposes the deviation. The setpoint remains in place; only the strength of the correction has changed.

cards.q: Which of these responses would be classified as positive feedback?
cards.a: A damaged vessel wall attracts platelets that release chemicals attracting still more platelets.
options: A damaged vessel wall attracts platelets that release chemicals attracting still more platelets
Rising body temperature increases sweating, which cools the body
A drop in plasma calcium triggers parathyroid hormone that raises calcium
A rise in carbon dioxide increases ventilation, which lowers carbon dioxide
cards.explanation: Platelet recruitment builds on itself, with each arriving platelet increasing the signal that brings in more, so the plug forms rapidly. Sweating, parathyroid hormone secretion, and the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide all reverse the change that triggered them, which makes them negative feedback.

cards.q: Why would positive feedback be a poor design for controlling body temperature?
cards.a: A small rise would drive temperature higher and higher instead of correcting it.
options: It would respond too slowly to be useful for temperature
A small rise would drive temperature higher and higher instead of correcting it
It would require a sensor, which the thermoregulatory system does not have
It would prevent the hypothalamus from changing the setpoint during illness
cards.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies deviation, so a warm day would push core temperature away from the survivable range rather than defend it, which is fatal within a narrow margin. Speed is not the problem; positive feedback is fast. The thermoregulatory system does have sensors in the skin and the hypothalamus. Setpoint resetting during fever is unrelated to the sign of the loop.

cards.q: In severe hemorrhage, cardiac output falls, coronary blood flow falls, the heart weakens, and cardiac output falls further. What is happening, and what does it imply for treatment?
cards.a: A positive feedback cycle has taken over, so an outside intervention such as restoring volume is required to break it.
options: Equilibrium has been reached, so cardiac output will hold at its new value
A negative feedback loop is correcting the problem, so no intervention is needed
The setpoint for cardiac output has been reset downward and the patient is stable
A positive feedback cycle has taken over, so an outside intervention such as restoring volume is required to break it
cards.explanation: Each fall in output worsens perfusion of the heart itself, which worsens output again, so the loop feeds itself and nothing internal can stop it. The baroreceptor reflex is trying to help, but once the vicious cycle dominates, the response no longer opposes the change. Cardiac output has no defended setpoint of its own that could be reset in this way. Equilibrium implies a stable resting state, which is not what a spiraling decline is.

cards.q: The sodium positive feedback of the action potential upstroke does not run forever. Which pair of events stops it?
cards.a: Inactivation of the sodium channels and delayed opening of potassium channels.
options: Inactivation of the sodium channels and delayed opening of potassium channels
A rise in extracellular sodium and closure of potassium channels
Activation of the Na+ K+ ATPase, which reverses the upstroke within a millisecond
A negative feedback sensor in the membrane detecting the peak voltage
cards.explanation: Sodium channels have a separate inactivation gate that closes shortly after opening, and voltage gated potassium channels open with a delay, so two processes outside the amplifying loop terminate it. Extracellular sodium does not change during a single spike, and closing potassium channels would prolong depolarization. The pump restores gradients over many cycles and is far too slow to end one upstroke. There is no voltage sensing comparator that halts the spike the way a homeostatic center would.

cards.q: A person with a fever of 39.5 C is given a drug that lowers the hypothalamic setpoint back to 37 C. Predict what the negative feedback loop does next.
cards.a: The system now reads 39.5 C as too high, so sweating and skin vasodilation begin and temperature falls.
options: Temperature rises further because lowering the setpoint amplifies the error
The person shivers harder because the body is still trying to reach 39.5 C
Nothing happens until the infection clears, since the setpoint cannot drive a response
The system now reads 39.5 C as too high, so sweating and skin vasodilation begin and temperature falls
cards.explanation: The integrating center compares actual temperature against the current setpoint, so lowering the target creates an error in the hot direction and triggers heat loss responses. Shivering would occur only if actual temperature were below the target, which is now not the case. The setpoint is precisely what drives the response, so the loop does not wait for the infection. Lowering a setpoint cannot amplify a deviation in a negative feedback system.

cards.q: Compare the ends of two loops: labor contractions and the baroreceptor response to standing up. Which statement is correct?
cards.a: Labor ends when the stimulus is physically removed, while the baroreceptor response shuts itself off as pressure returns to normal.
options: Labor ends when the stimulus is physically removed, while the baroreceptor response shuts itself off as pressure returns to normal
Both stop when their responses restore the original value of the variable
Both require an outside event, since no loop can stop on its own
The baroreceptor response ends only when the person lies back down, and labor stops on its own
cards.explanation: A negative feedback loop is self limiting because the response erases the error that drove it, while a positive feedback loop keeps building until something external interrupts it. Labor never restores the original state, so it cannot end by returning the variable to where it began. Negative feedback loops do stop on their own, which is exactly the difference. The baroreceptor reflex maintains pressure while standing rather than waiting for the person to lie down.

cards.q: What is feedforward control?
cards.a: A response made in anticipation of a change, before the regulated variable actually moves.
options: A slow structural change that develops over weeks in a new environment
A response triggered only after a sensor detects an error
A response made in anticipation of a change, before the regulated variable actually moves
A loop in which the response amplifies the original stimulus
cards.explanation: Feedforward uses a cue that predicts a disturbance and starts the correction early, which keeps the eventual deviation small. Responding after a detected error is ordinary negative feedback. A slow structural change over weeks is acclimatization. A response that amplifies the stimulus is positive feedback.

cards.q: What is acclimatization?
cards.a: A reversible physiological adjustment to a sustained change in the natural environment, developing over days to weeks.
options: An immediate reflex correction of a deviation
An anticipatory response triggered by a predictive cue
A permanent genetic change passed to offspring
A reversible physiological adjustment to a sustained change in the natural environment, developing over days to weeks
cards.explanation: Acclimatization involves changes in gene expression, hormone levels, and tissue properties that improve function in a new environment and fade when the person returns home. An immediate reflex correction is negative feedback and happens in seconds. Genetic change across generations is adaptation, which is evolutionary rather than physiological. An anticipatory response is feedforward.

cards.q: When does a feedforward response occur relative to the change in the regulated variable?
cards.a: Before the variable changes.
options: At the same instant the variable changes
Before the variable changes
Only after the variable has fully returned to its setpoint
Only when the variable moves outside its normal range
cards.explanation: The defining feature of feedforward is timing: the body reads a predictive cue and acts in advance, so the disturbance is blunted before it arrives. Acting at the same instant or after the deviation describes feedback. Waiting until the variable is back at the setpoint would leave nothing to correct. Waiting for the variable to leave its normal range is again feedback, and a late one.

cards.q: Which change occurs during acclimatization to high altitude over several weeks?
cards.a: Red blood cell production increases.
options: Plasma volume rises steadily above sea level values
Hemoglobin loses its ability to bind oxygen
Resting ventilation falls below sea level values
Red blood cell production increases
